articles.title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
articles.summary: For many locals on this island, the arrest has brought decades of frustration back to the fore.
articles.body:
For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there.

"Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC.

"Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"

Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments.

"I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC.

Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.

US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.

Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.

Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City.

The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha.

Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough.

"I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously."

"I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said.

Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough."

Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island.

The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime.

The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there.

In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government.

Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes.

In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store.

In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman.

"Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC.

"We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace."

articles.title: Teachers in Republic of Ireland begin industrial action
articles.summary: The teaching unions began work-to-rule action on Monday and there will be a full one-day strike on 14 October.
articles.body:
Primary and secondary school teachers across the Republic of Ireland have began industrial action over pay.

Two teaching unions, Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) and Irish National Teachers' Organisation (INTO), began work-to-rule action on Monday, and there will be a full one-day strike on 14 October.

INTO, which represents a majority of primary school teachers, has said schools "will be disrupted" as pre and post-school supervision will be withdrawn.

Members will also not attend staff meetings and parent-teacher meetings outside school hours.

The unions have said the Irish government has not made "meaningful commitments on pay" following the expiry of the last public sector pay deal at the end of June.

The industrial action comes as more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures last week .

Two days of fuller strike action have been planned for 14 and 21 October, when it is expected schools could be closed and picket lines formed across the country.

Members of another union, the Teachers' Union of Ireland (TUI), will begin industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule from 12 October.

The Irish government has said it is willing to enter talks but that it will not be held to a pre-determined outcome.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee's lawyer on Monday sent a legal notice to state-run SSKM Hospital and the Bangur Institute of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee's lawyer on Monday sent a legal notice to state-run SSKM Hospital and the Bangur Institute of Neurosciences over the alleged disclosure of her medical records from 2021 without the Trinamool Congress (TMC) supremo's permission, PTI reported.The development came two days after West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari alleged at a press conference in Kolkata that Mamata Banerjee had "faked" her leg injury during the 2021 state assembly elections, which the TMC eventually won.Also Read | 'No evidence of fracture': Bengal govt to probe Mamata Banerjee's 2021 'injury'Adhikari, a former Trinamool leader who joined the BJP in December 2020, displayed a document that he claimed was the March 11, 2021, report of the Bangur Institute of Neurosciences' Department of Radio Diagnosis. He said the report showed "no evidence of a fracture."Adhikari also announced that the state government would launch a fresh inquiry into what he described as Banerjee's "false claims" about her leg injury during the 2021 assembly election campaign.Following this, Mamata Banerjee's lawyer, Arka Nag, sent the notice to the director and medical superintendent of SSKM Hospital and the head of the neurology department at the Bangur Institute of Neurosciences.He sought an explanation as to how his client's medical records reached Adhikari and were subsequently made public. A copy of the notice was also sent to the principal secretary of the state health department.The notice referred to statements made by the chief minister on October 3 and argued that even if the medical records had been obtained by the state government or an investigating agency through a lawful process, that did not by itself authorise their disclosure to the public.It also sought to know whether the reports were disclosed pursuant to any court order and, if not, what action had been taken against those who provided the documents. The notice further sought clarification on whether the reports made public were the original medical records.The issue dates back to the 2021 West Bengal assembly election, when Mamata Banerjee, then chief minister and the TMC candidate from Nandigram, sustained injuries near Birulia Bazar while campaigning.She subsequently campaigned from a wheelchair, and the nature and extent of her injuries became a major political issue during the election.After the TMC returned to power, Mamata Banerjee, who at the time secure a third successive term as chief minister, was seen walking.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?
articles.summary: At least 23 huge data centres are planned in Scotland, causing significant concern for campaigners.
articles.body:
Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes.

Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale.

The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world.

Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres.

Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs.

Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make.

So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles?

From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse.

On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI.

While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering.

Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense.

One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife .

The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches.

AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves.

At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie , which has a capacity for 12MW.

The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level.

If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.

At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village.

noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems

The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.

The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium.

One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector.

Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed.

During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking.

As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating.

While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain.

An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead.

Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife.

What are the potential benefits of data centres?

As well as having a stake in a key future technology, those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs.

Lanarkshire has been designated an AI growth zone by the UK government, with data centres at its heart.

When it was announced in January , £8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs were promised.

The type of jobs a data centre creates has also been debated.

About 800 are expected to be in AI, with 50 apprenticeships. The rest are in construction.

Apatura - the developer behind 10 of the hyperscale data centre proposals in Scotland - highlights its green credentials with its access to renewable energy and battery storage.

With China and the US hoping to win the AI race, the UK government does not want to be left behind.

The Scottish government also supports the investment in the AI growth zone.

In August, it announced that ministers would have to be notified of proposed centres over 50MW in capacity.

A month later, it rejected the Scottish Greens' call for applications to be paused until new national guidelines are in force.

However, it said environmental impact assessments would have to be submitted.

The government also said it was "highly unlikely" any large data centres would be given the green light before Christmas, and promised that new guidance would be published by the festive season.

articles.title: Man arrested after creating AI crocodile image at Singapore reservoir; authorities shut water activities for 2 days and searched for reptile that never existed
articles.summary: A 30-year-old Myanmar national has been charged in Singapore after allegedly creating an AI-generated image showing a crocodile at Pandan Reservoir,
articles.body: A 30-year-old Myanmar national has been charged in Singapore after allegedly creating an AI-generated image showing a crocodile at Pandan Reservoir, triggering a real search for a reptile that did not exist. The image was sent to a colleague on August 20, after which Singapore’s national water agency PUB was alerted to the supposed sighting. PUB and the National Parks Board (NParks) launched search-and-capture operations, while water activities at the reservoir were suspended for two days. PUB later established that the photograph was fake and lodged a police report. The man, identified as Ye Lin, faces charges of communicating a false message and obstructing the course of justice. He has said he intends to plead guilty.AI crocodile image triggers reservoir searchThe incident began at about 3pm on August 20, when PUB received information that a crocodile had allegedly been spotted at Pandan Reservoir, accompanied by a photograph. Authorities treated the report as a potential public-safety concern and informed NParks. The agencies subsequently carried out search-and-capture operations around the reservoir. Warning signs were also placed in the area, advising members of the public to exercise caution.Water activities were suspended during the search. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were among those affected, with activities halted for two days. The search was eventually stopped after PUB established that the photograph was fake, and activities resumed on August 22.AI detection tools could not confirm the image was fakePUB later explained that it had used several AI-detection tools to examine the photograph. However, the tools produced inconclusive results, meaning they could not definitively establish whether the image had been generated or manipulated using AI.With the authenticity of the image uncertain, authorities opted to take precautionary measures rather than assume the reported crocodile was fictional. The incident demonstrates the practical challenge posed by increasingly realistic AI-generated images, particularly when they involve potential threats to public safety.Man allegedly created and shared the imagePolice investigations identified Ye Lin, 30, a Myanmar national, as the person who allegedly created the AI-generated crocodile image. According to police, Ye sent the image to a colleague, rather than publicly posting it online.Police also allege that Ye later deleted the AI-generated images and the log history from the Gemini AI application on his mobile phone. Investigators said this amounted to an attempt to conceal his actions and led to the separate allegation of obstructing the course of justice.PUB subsequently said Ye was employed by its reservoir-maintenance contractor. His supervisor was the person who alerted PUB to the image on August 20.Man faces two criminal chargesYe was charged on September 29 with communicating a false message under Section 14D of Singapore’s Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act 1906 and obstructing the course of justice under Section 204A of the Penal Code 1871.The false-message offence carries a maximum punishment of three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000, or both. The obstruction-of-justice offence carries a maximum sentence of seven years in prison, a fine, or both.The maximum prison terms for the two offences add up to 10 years. However, this does not mean Ye will automatically receive a 10-year sentence if convicted. The eventual punishment will depend on the court.Ye intends to plead guiltyYe appeared before Singapore’s State Courts on September 29 and, through an interpreter, said he intended to plead guilty. He also indicated that he would not engage a lawyer.His case is scheduled to return to court on November 10. As of October 5, no final sentence had been handed down.Police warn against AI-generated false informationSingapore Police have warned members of the public against circulating false information or manipulated images that could cause unnecessary alarm. Police specifically cautioned against submitting fabricated or manipulated material, including AI-generated or digitally altered images, to government agencies while presenting it as genuine.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two men die in English Channel crossing attempt off northern France
articles.summary: Two women were also rescued and taken to hospital with serious burns from the mixture of gasoline and seawater.
articles.body:
Two men have died after trying to cross the English Channel off the coast of Berck in northern France.

According to local media, police saw migrants leaving the beach on a boat at about 22:00 local time on Sunday, and when rescuers arrived, they were bailing water out of the overloaded vessel with their shoes.

"When we arrived, there were at least 80 people on board and a terrible smell of gasoline,"Jean-Marc Lamblin, director of the French national sea rescue service (SNSM) told La Voix du Nord newspaper.

Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns that were caused by the mixture of gasoline in the seawater. Their condition has been described as not life-threatening.

Lamblin told the newspaper that there were so many people on the boat, including children, that about 20 people were left stranded in the water because they could not get on board.

He explained that when SNSM arrived, the two men, aged in their 30s and 40s, were in cardiac arrest.

The men and injured women were brought back to shore where firefighters and paramedics helped them, but the men died at about midnight.

Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor's office has opened an investigation to determine the circumstances of their death.

The two women were from Somalia and aged 20 and 26, La Voix du Nord reported, adding that they are now recovering in Rang-du-Fliers hospital.

Separately, the UK Home Office said 149 migrants were picked up on Sunday in a mid-Channel rescue operation and were brought to Gosport, in Hampshire.

About 150 anti-migrant demonstrators had gathered at the south coast town to stop the group being brought ashore, with flares being set off and some scuffles with police.

Figures from the UK Home Office have recorded 19,451 people crossing the Channel in small boats this year.

The number is 43% lower than at the same time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

articles.summary: A 15-year-old student protesting against France’s dilapidated and understaffed schools lost his hand on Monday after picking up a police stun grenade in
articles.body: A 15-year-old student protesting against France’s dilapidated and understaffed schools lost his hand on Monday after picking up a police stun grenade in the northern town of Lens, a local official told reporters.An investigation has been opened into the incident, the official added.The incident came as hundreds of French schools entered a second consecutive week of closures, a day ahead of a nationwide day of nationwide demonstrations.About 400 to 500 high schools remained fully or partially closed on Monday out of a total of 3,700, French education minister Edouard Geffray said.According to Geffray, 24 schools had been burned or ransacked and 78 teaching staff had been injured since demonstrations began at a high school in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages before spreading nationwide.The protests come as the government of President Emmanuel Macron seeks to push through a deficit-reduction budget for 2027. France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5% last week, its highest level since 2002.Police-students clash in multiple citiesOn Monday, clashes broke out between police and students in Lille in northern France, the country's third-largest city, while tear gas was deployed in Toulouse in the southwest. Broadcaster BMFTV also showed a fire being lit as protesters attempted to break into a school in central Paris.Police and firefighters quickly extinguished the capital blaze. The school was evacuated and classes were suspended.Around 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested nationwide since last Monday, with dozens injured. Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while property damage is estimated to have reached tens of millions of euros.Paris police chief Patrice Faure, in an open letter published on X, claimed that those who initially launched the protests no longer had control over them and urged students to abandon blockades in favour of peaceful demonstrations.Student unions have nevertheless called for a nationwide day of demonstrations on Tuesday. Security officials fear that an organised protest, particularly in central Paris, could lead to further violence amid concerns that far-left and anarchist groups may attempt to take over the protests.CGT union chief Sophie Binet told TF1 television on Monday that CGT members would attend Tuesday's demonstrations "to protect high school students.""We've been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students," Binet said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027: Spring ticket resale, volunteering and line-up news
articles.summary: Those who missed out on Sunday should not lose hope, as there are other ways to secure a ticket.
articles.body:
Thousands of people were left disappointed on Sunday after tickets for Glastonbury Festival sold out in 42 minutes.

Organisers used a new booking system for the first time which entered people into a virtual waiting room. Despite having capacity for 210,000 people, demand is always much higher than supply.

But those who missed out on Sunday should not lose hope, as there are other ways to secure a ticket for the world-famous event when it returns to Worthy Farm in Somerset from 23-27 June.

Below is everything you need to know about how you can still secure a pass for the 2027 festival.

'My girl lost her limbs to meningitis - get the jab'

'Ageing without children can be hard and lonely'

Jeffrey Archer returns to his former school library

Have Glastonbury Festival 2027 tickets sold out?

Organisers confirmed that general admission tickets sold out in 42 minutes on Sunday.

Coach package tickets, which went on sale on Thursday, sold out in less than half an hour.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025.

In a statement on Instagram after the sale ended, organisers said: "Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in spring 2027."

How can I get tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027?

Tickets for the festival were sold exclusively by See Tickets and are strictly non-transferable.

Security will carry out thorough identification checks at all entry points on the site when the gates open to ensure validity.

Any tickets found to be bought through third parties will be cancelled and admission will be refused.

In a statement, organisers said: "If someone's claiming - whether on social media or elsewhere - they can get you Glastonbury tickets and it's not through See Tickets or directly from us, do not risk it."

They added that they are made aware of people "losing large sums of money" every year on fake tickets.

"Please do not fall victim to these scams," they said.

When can I buy a Glastonbury resale ticket?

Anybody who missed out at the general sale can attempt to buy resale tickets at a later date.

The sale will include cancelled or returned tickets.

An exact date is yet to be confirmed, but organisers said the sale will take place in spring.

Can I go to Glastonbury without a ticket?

The festival and its associated charities and organisations always need volunteers to help keep things running smoothly at Worthy Farm.

Normally, volunteers are required to work three eight-hour shifts in return for a pass to the festival, but the expectation does vary.

Oxfam has worked with Glastonbury for more than 25 years. Anybody hoping to volunteer with the charity can register their interest to join the 2,000-person team to work in roles on the gates, campaigning with the public or helping in the charity shop at the festival site.

Meanwhile, the Festaff stewarding team requires three eight-hour shifts per volunteer in return for a pass. According to the organisation, the shifts involve "light enjoyable customer facing tasks".

My Cause UK is looking for volunteers to work four shifts lasting six hours and 15 minutes with their Internal Traffic Management team.

There are also volunteer opportunities for the medical teams, tent stewards, campsite wardens and property lockups.

Aspiring volunteers have also been warned of fraudulent individuals and/or companies who claim to be recruiting.

Anybody unsure about the legitimacy of a company is advised to contact the festival.

When is the Glastonbury line-up announced?

Although the Glastonbury Festival 2027 line-up is yet to be announced, the rumours are rife already.

Emily Eavis, co-organiser of the festival, has already confirmed that Oasis will not be performing at Worthy Farm . Liam Gallagher posted on X that "it's not happening".

Eavis also told BBC Radio 4's programme that Madonna is "definitely not" headlining either.

She did reveal that three headliners were already lined up which the team was "very excited about" - but for now, we will have to wait and find out.

The last festival in 2025 was headlined by The 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo.

Those who were unlucky with Glastonbury tickets should fear not because the West Country offers a variety of other festivals throughout the summer:

Love Saves The Day - returns to Ashton Court Estate in Bristol 29-30 May

Bristol Sounds - returns to Canons Marsh Amphitheatre from 25 June

Forwards Festival - returns to Durdham Downs, dates to be confirmed

Cheltenham Jazz Festival - returns 28 April-3 May

Minety Music Festival - returns to the Cotswolds 1-4 July

Valley Fest - returns to Chew Valley 29 July-1 August

Shindig Festival - returns to Charlton Park Estate in Malmesbury 27-30 May

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into airport, reports suggest
articles.summary: The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
articles.body:
The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.

The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.

The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.

He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia.

Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster".

Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country

Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says

More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight – whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami – emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated.

Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport.

He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX – with more than 180 passengers on board – into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports.

The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government.

The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board.

There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities.

UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion.

Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.

Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.

He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.

Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.

Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure.

Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines.

But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency.

Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel".

Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017.

articles.title: Georgia officials hunt for suspect in shooting that killed two and injured 35
articles.summary: A homecoming celebration turned into a scene of deadly violence, as dozens of shots were fired into a crowd.
articles.body:
Investigators in the US state of Georgia are on the hunt for a suspect in a mass shooting that erupted in the early hours of Sunday, killing two people and injuring 35 more.

A crowd of roughly 1,000 people had gathered for a block party in the southern rural community of Vienna when, according to officials, more than 50 shots were fired.

Two of the victims were pronounced dead at the scene, while another 25 were transported to multiple nearby hospitals, some in critical condition.

No known arrests have been made and authorities have not given a possible motive for the violence. Victims ranged in age from 14 to 51.

The incident occurred on Sunday morning around 01:30 local time (05:30 GMT), during a Dooly High School homecoming celebration, though it was not a school-sponsored event.

"Our hearts are with the families grieving the loss of loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone affected by this tragedy," the school said in a statement.

Anticipating a large gathering, authorities from the Dooly County Sheriff's Office were already positioned at both ends of the crowd as gunfire rang out.

"Some people were reporting fireworks and then someone said somebody been shot," Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told local media.

Peavy said officials then worked their way through the crowd, as people ran scrambling in different directions, while authorities made their way towards victims.

Ashley Gee, who was there, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution news outlet that the barrage of gunfire sounded "like a machine gun".

Authorities arrived and found several people injured. The two deceased victims were found several blocks away from the scene of the shooting on Pine Street.

Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the two killed were both men, ages 20 and 23.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigations Medical Examiner's Office said it would conduct an autopsy in each case.

The bureau also said it would join the investigation at the request of the Dooly County Sheriff's Office, describing operations as "active and ongoing".

articles.title: BJP drops all 8 Uttar Pradesh Rajya Sabha members, including Hardeep Puri - what it means
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Monday named eight candidates for the Rajya Sabha elections from Uttar Pradesh, dropping all of its
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Monday named eight candidates for the Rajya Sabha elections from Uttar Pradesh, dropping all of its outgoing members from the state. Union petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri and Union minister of state for consumer affairs BL Verma also are among those who have not been renominated.The nominees, approved by the party's Central Election Committee, are Dharampal Singh, Radhakant Ojha, Prakash Pal, Vidyasagar Sonkar, Gopi Krishna Pandey, Priyanka Singh Rawat, Ram Pratap Singh Chauhan and Shruti Gangwar. Voting for 10 UP seats is on October 16, and the last date for filing nominations is October 6.The outgoing BJP members, apart from Hardeep Singh Puri and BL Verma, are Arun Singh, Neeraj Shekhar, Geeta Shakya, Brijlal and Seema Dwivedi.The eighth seat belonged to former deputy chief minister Dinesh Sharma, who resigned on September 11 after being appointed lieutenant governor (LG) of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. His term was due to end on November 25, like those of the others.Meanwhile, the move has set the ball rolling for different interpretations ahead of the UP assembly polls and the long speculated Union cabinet reshuffle as no sitting BJP member from the state was retained. Puri's name had been widely discussed for renomination, as had that of former Union minister Smriti Irani, who is also absent from the list.It is seen as a move motivated by the 2027 assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh, which the party will contest to form government for the third time in the state. The list, inevitably, appears to have names chosen to balance social, regional and caste combinations.The three candidates in the list are from the upper castes, three from Other Backward Classes (OBC) and two from Scheduled Castes. Ojha and Pandey, both Brahmins, are among the upper-caste picks. Dharampal Singh, a Lodhi, replaces outgoing MP BL Verma, who belongs to the same community. The list also spans Pal and Kurmi communities. Two women, Gangwar and Rawat, are among the nominees.The party seems to have leaned towards grassroots and organisational leaders rather than prominent national faces with the induction of Dharampal Singh, an animal husbandry minister in CM Yogi Adityanath's government.BJP is learnt to have zeroed in on at least 100 MLAs who are reportedly facing anti-incumbency at the ground level and a large number of them may be denied the ticket to contest the UP Assembly elections next year.Sources said this data has emerged after an on-ground assessment done by the party in 255 seats represented by BJP in the UP Assembly.A top UP BJP member confirmed to TOI that about 100 MLAs are on the radar following reports of lack of trust in them among voters. Friction with the organisational brass at the local level is also being accounted for while flagging these legislators, the senior member said. Sources said that feedback has also been taken from RSS vis-à-vis the candidacy of the sitting MLAs.Cabinet reshuffle on cards?The BJP's decision not to renominate Union petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri and Union minister of state BL Verma has also fuelled speculation that a Union cabinet reshuffle could be on the cards.Under Article 75(5) of the Constitution, a minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for six consecutive months must cease to hold office. With Puri and Verma's Rajya Sabha terms ending on November 25, their omission from the UP list raises questions over whether the two will be given another route into Parliament or whether the BJP is preparing for a wider reshuffle. The party, however, has not indicated what the move means for either minister.Also beyond Uttar Pradesh, the BJP on Sunday named Dinesh Arya for the Uttarakhand seat and Trinamool Congress (TMC) defector Rukmini "Koel" Mallick for the West Bengal bypoll. In the March round of Rajya Sabha elections, it fielded its unit chiefs in Bihar and Odisha and retained one sitting MP in Odisha.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cardiff half marathon runner dies
articles.summary: Event organisers confirm a participant has died and thanked medical teams working during the race.
articles.body:
A runner has died after taking part in Cardiff Half Marathon.

Event organisers Run4Wales said on Monday that the participant had died, adding: "We'd like to acknowledge the event and hospital medical teams who reacted with great speed and professionalism.

"Our deepest sympathies go out to the runner's family and friends."

It said no further details would be released "in respect of the family's wishes".

Sunday's race was the 23rd edition of the the 13.1 mile (21km) route, which saw about 30,000 people take to the streets .

In 2024, 37-year-old Stephen Jenkins died in hospital after collapsing at the finish line .

In 2019, Ben McDonald, 25, and Dean Fletcher, 32, crossed the finish line within minutes of each other, and both died after going into cardiac arrest .

Cardiff Half Marathon is Wales' largest mass participant and multi-fundraising event, with more than £4m raised each year for charity.

It's the UK's second largest half marathon and a member of the SuperHalfs, a global series of the world's most prestigious half marathons including races in Lisbon, Prague, Berlin, Copenhagen and Valencia. It has also been awarded a Elite Race Label by World Athletics.

articles.title: ‘SC itself scheduled, then cancelled meeting’: One Nation, One Election JPC chief PP Chaudhary amid controversy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: 'One nation, one election' JPC chief and BJP MP PP Chaudhary on Monday gave a clarification amid the, now cancelled, proposed meeting of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: 'One nation, one election' JPC chief and BJP MP PP Chaudhary on Monday gave a clarification amid the, now cancelled, proposed meeting of the parliamentary panel with Supreme Court judges, saying that it was SC that called the meeting and then cancelled it.Chaudhary claimed that Supreme Court had set the meeting for October 6 at 4.30 PM via an email sent to the committee’s Director on September 22.“Many members were not aware that the Supreme Court itself had scheduled the meeting. Through an email dated the 22nd, the Supreme Court informed our Director that it had fixed the meeting for the 6th at 4:30 PM. When the Supreme Court later cancelled the meeting, we also cancelled it and issued a notice to all the members. Since the meeting had initially been scheduled by the Supreme Court, we had informed all members accordingly,” he added, as quoted by ANI.Chaudhary further said the proposed interaction was informal and there was no reason to attach undue significance to it. He also pointed to previous instances of discussions between parliamentary committees and the judiciary. "The committee and the Supreme Court also said that if it is not appropriate, this issue should not be escalated. If both sides can hold a discussion, that is fine; if not, that is fine as well. There is no need to lay so much stress on this matter or blow it out of proportion," he said, speaking to ANI after the JPC meeting, held earlier in the day.He cited previous committee proceedings to argue that such interactions were not unprecedented."Earlier, regarding committee matters like the Education Bill and several others, as Mr Wilson stated, he had advised the committee to discuss matters with them. There are several past precedents of holding discussions with the Supreme Court. So there was nothing wrong with it either. And if the Supreme Court did not consider it appropriate, there is no issue at all," Chaudhary said.Further talking about the release of its report, he added, "Look, the process is currently ongoing; we are hearing the stakeholders. Once all members convey that there is no further need to hear anyone, and after gathering the opinions of all the members, we will submit the report,."The clarification came after former Union minister and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal criticised the proposed interaction, calling it "unconstitutional". Sibal had said the separation of powers under the Constitution meant that courts, rather than Parliament, determine the constitutionality of legislation."I have never heard in the history of India till date that a parliamentary group holds a meeting in the Supreme Court regarding a law (One Nation One Election), to tell the Supreme Court judges what this law actually is. I am talking about 'One Nation One Election'... I have never heard of such a thing in my legal career. This is unconstitutional," Sibal said at a press conference.The JPC is examining the Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024 and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024, which seek to provide the statutory framework for synchronising elections to the Lok Sabha, state assemblies and Union Territory assemblies.Chaudhary also referred to a letter by DMK MP P Wilson, saying there were precedents for such interactions. "You will receive the details regarding that. It has happened in the past. It is stated in Mr Wilson's letter; he placed that letter before the committee," he said.The JPC met at the Parliament Library Building in New Delhi on Monday as it continued its deliberations on the two Bills. Chaudhary said the committee was still in the process of hearing stakeholders and would submit its report once members were satisfied that all necessary views had been heard.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Twelve arrests after Gosport protest over migrant boat arrival
articles.summary: Flares were set off and there were a few scuffles with police during the stand-off in Gosport.
articles.body:
Twelve people have been arrested for offences including assaulting a police officer after a protest over migrant arrivals in a south coast town.

The Home Office said 149 migrants had been picked up in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI, alongside a French vessel, and were brought ashore at Gosport.

Flares were set off and there were scuffles with police during the stand-off at a marina in the Hampshire town, involving about 150 anti-migrant demonstrators on Sunday.

Eleven men and one woman were arrested on suspicion of offences including assaulting police officers, affray and racially aggravated public order. All remain in custody.

The migrants were taken by coach to a processing centre in Kent.

It is the second known landing of large numbers of migrants this far west along the south coast in recent years.

A police cordon was in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful.

Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot".

Hampshire Police said it had deployed officers to "support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea", including the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, RNLI, and Border Security Command.

The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act, as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings.

A small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured, police said.

Assistant Chief Constable Simon Dodds said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

"Our position on this has been clear that we will investigate thoroughly and take robust action against anyone responsible.

"Last night saw a number of incidents that were clearly not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He said officers "did not deserve to be assaulted as they worked incredibly diligently" to ensure the "safety of everyone in the area".

"Neither do they, or anyone from our partner agencies, deserve to be singled out online or subjected to abuse via social media," he said.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made.

"We will continue to review body-worn video footage and videos posted online to identify any further offences and may make further arrests in due course in required".

A 36-year-old man from Bognor Regis on suspicion of assaulting a police officer, failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction and failing to comply with the conditions of a dispersal order

A 38-year-old man from Fareham on suspicion of failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction

A 45-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of assaulting a police officer, criminal damage and being drunk and disorderly in a public place

A 29-year-old man from Portsmouth on suspicion of assaulting a police officer and failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction

A 56-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of assaulting a police officer.

A 22-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of affray and racially aggravated public order

A 42-year-old man from Fareham on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in a public place and failing to comply with the conditions of a dispersal order

A 35-year-old man on suspicion of assault by beating of an emergency worker and failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction

A 39-year-old man from Emsworth on suspicion of criminal damage, attempted criminal damage and possession of a pyrotechnic article at a protest

A 57-year-old woman from Emsworth on suspicion of assaulting a police officer

A 59-year-old man from Gosport on suspicion of racially aggravated public order

A 29-year-old man of no fixed address on suspicion of obstruction of a highway after ambulances were prevented from travelling along Clayhall Road

Five people were also issued with Section 35 dispersal notices.

A Home Office spokesperson refused to explain why Gosport had been chosen on this occasion, saying they do not comment on "operational processes".

"The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border," they said.

They said it was "vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival".

It is the third crossing in a month. So far this year 19,451 people are recorded as having crossed the Channel in small boats.

That number is 43% lower than this time last year, and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

Last month, more than 100 migrants landed at Eastney, in Portsmouth, leading to more scuffles between police and demonstrators .

articles.title: Anger in Japan grows after US Marine is arrested over the killing of a woman on Okinawa
articles.summary: Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman on Okinawa has drawn condemnation from Japan's leaders and renewed protests against the heavy Americ...
articles.body:
TOKYO (AP) — The arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman on Okinawa has drawn condemnation from Japan's leaders and renewed protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern island.

The alleged killing could complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to strengthen Japanese military defense on the island and to work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China in the region.

Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.

Security camera footage showed a man wearing a black top, trousers and white sneakers entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.

Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.

"I'm outraged and flabbergasted to hear that a suspect came to the (entertainment area) after committing a murder," Kenji Higa, who lives in Okinawa City, told the Okinawa Times.

There is longstanding anger over the behavior of some Americans

People in Okinawa have long been wary of the U.S. presence on the island but many have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China.

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today.

There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.

After the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members, huge crowds protested the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. There was also anger over the rape of a teenage girl by a U.S. service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime.

About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, condemning the crime and renewing demands that U.S. military bases be removed from the island.

One sign read: "We've had enough of this!"

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."

Koja said the case underscored the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes.

"I'm enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident," Koja told Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and U.S. Consul General in Naha, Andrew Ou on Monday when he summoned them to the prefectural government. He demanded that U.S. officials take effective preventive measures.

Watson replied: "I recognize the serious incident caused significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbors" and that "we are committed to being good neighbors … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people."

In Tokyo, Takaichi condemned the crime and demanded full cooperation and tougher disciplinary and preventive measures by the United States.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi also summoned U.S. Forces Japan Commander Lt. Gen. Stephen Jost to his ministry, while Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi expressed his outrage to the U.S. ambassador to Japan, George Glass.

Glass, on X, expressed his condolences Sunday to the victim's family and said the United States is cooperating with Japanese authorities.

On Monday, he said he is telling U.S. military commanders of the need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity" and that he and Watson discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."

Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.

Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in coming weeks.

If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

articles.title: 'Beyond limits': Ex-CJI Gavai, former judges slam SC judge Ujjal Bhuyan's remarks amid EC-SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Chief Justice of India BR Gavai and other retired judges on Monday condemned Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan's remarks on the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Chief Justice of India BR Gavai and other retired judges on Monday condemned Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan's remarks on the Election Commission.Gavai said that a sitting judge should not have made comments on the ongoing row over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls as the matter is sub judice before the top court."Judicial propriety would not permit him to make any comment on the matter which is sub judice before the court," Gavai told news agency PTI.Retired Delhi high court judges SN Dhingra and RS Sodhi also questioned Bhuyan's remarks.Justice Dhingra said Bhuyan's statement was "way beyond the limits of a sitting top court judge" and such comments should not be made at a public event when the issue is pending before the same court."He should have thought a thousand times before making such a statement," Dhingra said, adding that Justice Bhuyan did not know the full facts of the issue.Justice R S Sodhi also criticised Justice Bhuyan for calling the SIR exercise disenfranchisement and said that the right to vote was governed by the statutory framework."Whether you have a vote or you don't have a vote depends upon the statute. If you fall within the parameters of the statute, you have a vote. If you don't fall within the parameters of the statute, you don't have a vote," Justice Sodhi said."I mean, these hardline thinking and these hardline statements, to my mind, are not a very mature way of looking at a thing, especially when you are supposed to be in a field which is supposed to be excellent in its rationalising," he said.What Bhuyan had saidThis comes a day after Justice Bhuyan said that any process that "disenfranchises" millions of Indian citizens was "intrinsically arbitrary" and a "negation" of the constitutional order.While delivering the valedictory address at the 19th Justice Bodh Raj Sawhney Memorial Moot Court Competition at NALSAR University of Law on Sunday, Justice Bhuyan said that the Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens, one with voting rights and the other without voting rights, and no amount of "whataboutery" could justify such a process.“If any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary. No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of the Constitution and I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution of India,” Bar and Bench quoted Justice Bhuyan as saying.He said the Constitution does not create two classes of citizens based on voting rights and added that wholesale disenfranchisement would violate Articles 326 and 14.“No authority can do it; no court can condone it. No one is above the Constitution,” he said.This is not the first time that Justice Bhuyan has put forth his views on issues being discussed in the public domain.Recently, NALSAR Hyderabad was in the news after a section of its students wrote to the vice chancellor, registrar and professors of the institution, opposing any proposal to invite Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as chief guest to the varsity's convocation.Justice Bhuyan, who served as the Chancellor of NALSAR, on Sunday said he can be legitimately proud of the students of the institution."You have shown to the country and the world what a university student, that too, a student of law, should be like. You are brilliant. You are bold and you are brave," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Eryn Bonner: Arizona State cheerleader slammed to the ground by cops in viral video, charged for hindering police
articles.summary: An Arizona State University student has been charged with two misdemeanors months after her video with cops went viral.
articles.body: An Arizona State University student has been charged with two misdemeanors months after her video with cops went viral. On July 19, officers were going to arrest a man on Mill Avenue in downtown Tempe. Eryn Kelise Bonner, 21, an ASU senior and member of the university's Stunt Team, resisted the arrest and was slammed to the ground by the officers. Tempe police alleged that Bonner punched an officer multiple times and then cops had to restrain her. A bodycam footage from the arrest showed that the officer tossed Bonner onto a bicycle and restrained her. The officer punched her while another handcuffed her.Bonner had now been slapped with two misdemeanor charges of disorderly conduct and hindering or interfering with police -- while her family was shocked that she was charged after being beaten up by a cop.“There are no words to fully describe the heartbreak of watching our daughter being hurt by someone entrusted to protect and serve our community,” the Bonner family said. “The hardest thing is seeing the pain and sadness in her eyes that we cannot take away,” the statement continued. “Expecting public servants to live up to the highest standards of their profession is not an act of animosity toward those who serve with honor.”Bonner was left with bruises after the encounter.The complete body-camera and surveillance footage released by Tempe police has become central to the dispute. While the short social-media clip sparked concerns about the officer's use of force, police have argued that the longer footage provides additional context and shows Bonner repeatedly ignoring commands to move away from the arrest. The Tempe Officers Association has also said the footage shows Bonner striking and scratching an officer.Attorney Benjamin Taylor, who represents the Bonner family,said the cop who touched Bonner should be fired.“This was very extreme, very excessive and there was no need for double pushes, jumping on top and multiple strikes,” Taylor said. “The city of Tempe would be very vindictive to try to charge her again after they see what this officer did,” Taylor said.“If you look at the end of the video, there’s some odd touching at the end of the video which is very concerning,” he said. “At the end you see his hand go on her buttocks which is very odd in this situation.”“Rather, it is essential to preserving public trust and upholding the integrity and legitimacy of our institutions. articles.title: Rachel Jupp announced as BBC's new director of news after Deborah Turness exit
articles.summary: Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor.
articles.body:
Rachel Jupp has been appointed the new director of BBC News, nearly a year after the previous CEO resigned.

Deborah Turness announced last November that she would step down from the role following the fallout over how Panorama edited a speech by President Trump.

Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor, but left several years before the controversial Trump episode aired.

In a statement, Jupp said she was "honoured to be asked to lead BBC News", while the corporation's director-general Matt Brittin described her as "an outstanding editorial leader".

The appointment comes as the BBC continues to make sweeping cuts to its news division. Around 550 job closures have been announced so far , with more expected to follow.

The BBC as a whole will cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save £500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

In a statement, Brittin said Jupp was "widely regarded for her news judgement, fairness and high standards".

"She brings a clarity of vision for the future, and the determined, collaborative approach needed to strengthen BBC News," he added.

Jupp joined Channel 4 News in 2005 and served as the programme's head of home news, before moving to the BBC in 2013 to become Newsnight's deputy editor in 2013.

She became the editor of Panorama in 2016, a position she held for the next four years.

Jupp also served as editorial executive for BBC Content, and more recently has led the BBC's editorial work on generative AI, based in the US.

In her statement, Jupp said: "I want to champion our vital, independent and impartial journalism, deepen the trust people have in the BBC and meet our audiences wherever they are.

"I'm grateful to Matt for this opportunity, and I'm looking forward to working with our dedicated, brilliant teams across the UK and around the world."

The BBC's cuture and media editor Katie Razzall said it was "significant" that Brittin had chosen someone with experience of using artificial intelligence to run his news teams, "raising questions around how AI could open up the next frontier of a modern newsroom".

The BBC said Jupp would be paid a salary of £400,000. Turness started on a similar salary in 2022, but that had increased to between £445,000 and £449,999 in her last year before leaving the role.

Jupp will have responsibility for about 4,500 staff, and also serve as a member of the BBC's executive committee.

Jonathan Munro, who has been acting as interim head of the news division for the last 11 months, will return to his role as deputy director of BBC News when Jupp takes up her role.

Brittin said: "I would like to thank Jonathan Munro for his professionalism and leadership of BBC News in the past 11 months. I have been personally grateful for his deep experience, calm head and steady hand."

The director general said BBC News remained the most used and most trusted news provider around the world and across the UK, but added that it faced significant challenges.

"In a world of infinite choice, audiences are fragmenting, trust is scarce and facts are contested," Brittin said.

"It is our duty to recommit to the BBC's distinctive journalistic mission while reinventing how we serve audiences, and to rise to these challenges. In Rachel, we have someone who can do both, with a fresh persepctive to lead BBC News into a new era."

Jupp's predecessor Turness left the BBC after an internal memo leaked to the Telegraph highlighted that an episode of Panorama broadcast a year earlier had edited a speech by President Trump in a misleading way.

In her letter of resignation, Turness said: "While mistakes have been made, I want to be absolutely clear recent allegations that BBC News is institutionally biased are wrong."

The BBC's then-director general Tim Davie also resigned over the scandal, and was replaced by Brittin earlier this year.

The episode of Panorama spliced together two sections of a speech he delivered in 2021, shortly before the Capitol riots on 6 January.

President Trump launched a $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the BBC after the edit came to light.

The BBC apologised and said the edit had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action", but rejected his demand for compensation.

The case is currently scheduled to go to trial in the US in 2027.

articles.title: Tennessee’s outgoing prison chief had a history of execution missteps before Christa Pike, officials say
articles.summary: Before the botched execution of Christa Pike, Frank Strada reportedly had a history of overseeing execution missteps in two states.
articles.body:
Before the botched execution of Christa Pike, Frank Strada reportedly had a history of overseeing execution missteps in two states.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Saturday announced Correction Commissioner Strada would step down later this month following the backlash after the attempted execution left Pike on a ventilator, unconscious in a hospital. Less than three years earlier, Lee brought Strada on to lead the Department of Correction, tasking him with reforming Tennessee's execution system after enduring concerns over the state's approach to the death penalty.

But in Strada's previous role as an official in Arizona's prisons system, he oversaw three executions that administrators and observers raised concerns over, saying executioners flouted the state's official policies. Now under his current supervision, Pike is the second person this year who Tennessee officials have failed to execute after problems with the IV injections.

The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment when asked by CNN about Strada's involvement in these prior execution problems.

Pike's debilitating survival has brought to light Strada's history overseeing executions that didn't follow typical protocol, and larger questions about the death penalty by both proponents and opponents. Lee has suspended executions for the year as an investigation is underway.

"The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing, so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that's what they want to be done in their name," Stephen Ferrell, Pike's lawyer, told CNN's Jake Tapper on Sunday. "This torturous execution leaves so many questions that the state of Tennessee will refuse to answer."

As his resignation was announced, Strada said, "stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."

"I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary," Strada said in a statement Saturday, "and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred."

Here's the latest on Strada's final days overseeing Tennessee's prisons, and what happened inside Pike's death chamber.

Prisons chief oversaw past execution mishaps in Arizona

On Saturday, the state Attorney General's Office retained Ed Stanton, a former US attorney, to conduct an independent review of the Department of Correction's actions in carrying out Pike's execution, Gov. Lee's office announced.

Stanton previously oversaw an independent review of Tennessee's lethal injection protocol in 2022, the governor's office said, which resulted in the state substantially rewriting its protocol.

Strada began leading Tennessee's correction department in 2023 when he was tasked with enacting that new protocol among other duties. An Air Force veteran, Strada was a senior official in Arizona's prison system who previously had worked nearly 30 years for the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

In naming Strada to lead the agency , Lee said Strada's "extensive corrections management and law enforcement experience make him well-suited to lead the Department of Correction."

Strada served as a deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry. His tenure was marked with controversy around three executions that were performed after an eight-year moratorium in the state.

All three had issues with establishing IV lines to administer the lethal drug, lawyers said. The problems prompted Arizona's governor to call for an independent review of execution protocols. The review in Arizona was announced weeks after Lee promoted Strada to his current post in Tennessee.

In a 2023 sworn declaration, Ryan Thornell, director of Arizona's corrections department, said he was "unable to locate sufficient documentation" about execution procedures under the previous administration, which included Strada. He cited "several critical issues" impacting the agency's ability to conduct executions, including inadequate expertise, efficacy of lethal injection drugs, and procedures with the IV team.

Thornell said he couldn't find documentation identifying the pharmacist who compounded the lethal drugs. Without naming Strada, he said a prior deputy director was the main point of contact with the pharmacist but said he didn't record anything. The effectiveness of the current supplies of the lethal drug couldn't be guaranteed and needed to be tested to ensure safety and efficacy prior to use, Thornell said.

Meanwhile, he said the IV team who worked on the state's most recent execution had been told by the prior administration to only use the femoral central line, which was against the department's policy.

Two failed execution attempts in Tennessee

In Tennessee, questions have mounted around the Department of Correction's protocol around executions, including IV administration to administer lethal doses.

Pike's case wasn't the first time state officials had trouble with lethal injections in recent months. In May, state officials halted the execution of Tony Carruthers when staff couldn't get a secondary IV successfully placed after placing one IV into his right arm.

Later, the state's execution of Anthony Darrell Hines was performed in August without any reported issues with placing the IVs, according to The Associated Press.

Laura Porter, the executive director of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said attorneys and community leaders in Tennessee have been trying to get the state government to "take seriously the huge problems with the competency of the state's execution process."

"They were ignored. Hopefully, this is the beginning of accountability and an end to secrecy that enables these debacles," Porter said Saturday in an emailed statement reacting to Strada's resignation.

Other advocates say the issues with Tennessee's procedures speak to larger issues around the death penalty.

"It's not isolated to just one particular person or one particular execution team," Kat Jutras, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Alternatives for Arizona, told CNN. "If we look at it in that very microlens, we're not seeing the broader picture with the death penalty itself and lethal injections really being at the forefront of some of the larger problems."

Attempting another execution won't bring justice, her lawyer tells CNN

Pike, who along with her boyfriend was convicted for the 1995 torture and killing of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, was one of the youngest women sent to death row.

During her scheduled execution Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, executioners struggled to set the IV lines necessary to administer the lethal dose of pentobarbital. Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, told reporters she cooperated with the execution team and tried to give them tips on how to insert the IV lines, as she had warned the state she had a history with difficult vein access.

But her lawyers said issues with the IV resulted in the barbiturate, which slows the central nervous system, flowing into her body instead of her bloodstream. After the first dose failed to work, executioners administered a second dose.

"We may never know what sort of torture she endured during that process," Ferrell, an assistant federal defender in Tennessee, said on CNN's "State of the Union." It's unclear whether she was conscious or in physical pain during the procedure and subsequent life-saving treatment, he added.

"We don't know what the prognosis is, as in the long-term prognosis, if she recovers," he said, saying she remained unconscious in the hospital as of Sunday morning. "She may not fully recover."

Her lawyers have called on the governor to commute Pike's death sentence. After being convicted of first-degree murder, Pike has served more than 30 years in prison, mostly in solitary confinement, only to be brought out for a failed execution, Ferrell said.

"This has been a serious punishment for a very serious and awful crime," Ferrell said. "I don't think that attempting another execution is going to bring justice."

The state Attorney General's Office hasn't given an indication of whether they'll seek to put her to death again, he added.

Gov. Lee, who is term-limited after serving for eight years, will leave office in January. Republican US Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is running to replace him, has called to bring back the electric chair to "deliver justice for these victims swiftly."

Some Tennessee lawmakers, including state House Speaker Cameron Sexton , have also proposed allowing the firing squad as an alternative execution method. At least five states have authorized the use of a firing squad for the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center .

'State owes me a big apology,' victim's mother says

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told CNN affiliate WTLV/First Coast News she believes the state failed her family, more than three decades after Pike killed Slemmer, who was 19.

"I think the state owes me a big apology," she said.

Traveling from Florida with her husband, Martinez spent hours at the Nashville-area prison waiting to see Pike's execution. But the curtains eventually closed in the execution area and witnesses had to leave. They were later told Pike was being taken to the hospital, Martinez said.

Martinez said she worries about Pike being out and said her family hasn't been told whether her daughter's murderer will return to prison.

Now she, along with state officials, must wait for answers to lingering questions of what went wrong with the execution and what's next for Pike.

CNN's Dakin Andone, Eric Levenson, Lauren del Valle and Ryan Young contributed to this report.

articles.title: Artist 'taking legal advice' over Tories' use of Andy Burnham portrait
articles.summary: Manchester illustrator Stan Chow says he was not asked permission for use of his  cartoon.
articles.body:
An artist has said he is taking legal advice after accusing the Conservative Party of copying his portrait of Andy Burnham at their party conference.

People attending the party's conference in Birmingham have been handed water bottles featuring the image and labelled "Bottler Burnham" and "0% strength".

Labour supporter Stanley Chow, who created the image for Burnham's 2021 mayoral campaign in Greater Manchester, has claimed the party did not ask for permission to use the image.

A Conservative Party spokeswoman said the bottles were were not on sale and merely handed out to attending media in "goody bags".

Manchester illustrator Chow said: "I was stunned and angry when I saw what they had done. It is childish from them. I am taking legal advice.

"I'm very disappointed. It's frustrating that an institution like the Conservative Party has no idea that they are infringing copyright."

The artist claimed Reform UK had also infringed his copyright by using the image a few months ago in AI-generated social media campaign posts.

A Reform UK spokesman said at the time that it had "removed the posts in good faith and without any admission of liability on our part".

Brit Awards art trail turns streets into a gallery

Meet Stanley Chow - the football illustrator

Chow said: "I can't quite believe the Tories are resorting to this too.

"Regardless of your political allegiance, what the Tories have done is still copyright infringement.

"Ultimately, I want to raise awareness that you can't just take someone else's artwork and do what you want with it.

"I want to show other artists that when this does happen, you can make a stand, especially in this day and age where artists are struggling, because of AI and the cost of living."

Chow's image of Burnham has been used extensively by the politician across a series of campaigns and was recently used by the now-PM when he stood for election in Makerfield in June.

Manchester United fan Chow is well-known for his portraits of famous faces and he has previously created images of footballers, including Wayne Rooney, Edgar Davids and Ronaldinho.

He has also exhibited a series of portraits of "Great Northerners", which featured the likes of actress Maxine Peake, suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay, and recently curated an art trail for the Brit Awards' arrival in his home city.

He has also drawn Eric Cantona and presented a picture of Sir Alex Ferguson to the former Red Devils manager.
