articles.title: 'What's the purpose of SIR if citizens are removed?' Bombay high court's Goa bench raps EC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court's Goa bench on Monday \"reminded\" the Election Commission of India (ECI) that \"it has an obligation to ensure that
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court's Goa bench on Monday "reminded" the Election Commission of India (ECI) that "it has an obligation to ensure that eligible Indian citizens are included" in the final electoral roll, questioning the purpose of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) if voters are being removed from the list."But what are you doing? If citizens are being removed from the list then what is the purpose of this entire SIR process?" a division bench of Justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit Jamsandekar, was quoted as saying by Live Law.The court's remarks came while examining concerns over voter deletions during the SIR exercise. The bench referred to observations made by the Supreme Court that ensuring the inclusion of Indian citizens in the final voter list is the ECI's responsibility.The comments was in the backdrop of the wider legal challenge to the voter revision exercise, with concerns being raised over the manner in which names could be excluded from electoral rolls.Maharashtra HC declines urgent interventionMeanwhile, the Bombay high court's principal bench in Mumbai refused to pass an urgent interim order stopping the deletion of voters' names in Maharashtra under the SIR process.A bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said the issue was already before the Supreme Court and that it would not be appropriate for the high court to conduct parallel proceedings or issue orders on the matter.The court was hearing a petition filed by Sagar Ramesh Gawai, youth wing president of the Vanchit Bahujan Aghadi, founded by former MP Prakash Ambedkar.The petition alleges procedural violations and arbitrary exclusion of voters during the door-to-door enumeration exercise being carried out as part of the SIR in Maharashtra. It has also sought greater transparency and compliance with provisions of the Representation of the People Act.Petition seeks safeguards before voter deletionThe petitioner has opposed unilateral deletion of names from electoral rolls and sought a formal hearing before an Electoral Registration Officer, followed by a reasoned or speaking order, before any voter is removed.Senior advocate Ashutosh Kumbhakoni, appearing for the ECI, told the court that the Supreme Court is scheduled to hear the SIR matter concerning Maharashtra and other states and Union Territories on October 8.The high court said it would amount to judicial impropriety to examine the same issue simultaneously. It also noted that the Supreme Court had specifically requested High Courts not to conduct parallel proceedings concerning the SIR exercise.Prakash Ambedkar, appearing for the petitioner, sought an interim direction preventing any further deletion of names from the electoral rolls. The high court declined to grant the relief at this stage and posted the matter for hearing after three weeks.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: St Giles' Cathedral introduces fee for visitors outside Scotland
articles.summary: St Giles' Cathedral now charges an entrance fee for visitors from outside Scotland.
articles.body:
Visitors from outside Scotland now need to pay to enter one of Edinburgh's most popular attractions for the first time in its 900-year history.

General admission to St Giles' Cathedral is set at £12, while free entry is still offered to Scottish residents and under-16s.

Scottish visitors can get into the historic cathedral for free by registering online and providing proof of residency, while visitors who live elsewhere in the UK or abroad will need to pay for tickets.

Located on the capital's historic Royal Mile, the cathedral welcomes more than 1.5 million visitors each year.

St Giles': Playing a part in history for 900 years

St Giles was first founded in 1124 as a Catholic cathedral but later became a key site during the spread of Presbyterianism in Scotland when reformer John Knox was elected as its minister in 1560.

It remains a key site for major ceremonial events, including the public viewing of the late Queen's coffin in 2022 and the Kirking of the Scottish Parliament, while also hosting Sunday services.

While it is the first time the cathedral has charged for entry, other religious sites in the UK have introduced similar fee mechanisms.

York Minster charges £20 for general admission tickets and under-18s can accompany paying adults for free, while St Paul's Cathedral in London charges a £26 fee for tourist visits, while permitting service attendees free entry.

More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East

According to the St Giles' Cathedral charity trust, the site's annual operational costs are more than £1m.

The charity, which manages the cathedral, said it did not receive regular funding from the Scottish government or local council and had decided to introduce the entry charge to ensure the site can continue its long-term operation as a visitor attraction, religious site and cultural centre.

Alongside providing funding for the day-to-day operation of the building and its religious services, the entrance charge will allow the charity to expand its cultural offerings, according to Jack Oades the cathedral's organist and head of music, said.

Oades said the additional funding "will allow us to significantly level-up our musical offering and our in-house concerts and events".

"This will not only allow us to improve the frequency of our choral worship, but to attract world-class performers and engage with the wider creative and cultural activities across Edinburgh and Scotland," he added.

The Reverend Dr Scott Rennie, who took over as the minister of St Giles in May, said: "As Scotland's High Kirk we want to offer visitors from home and abroad the best possible experience and the opportunity to understand how faith and history have shaped Scotland's life as a nation.

"I am confident that these changes will be transformational in incorporating the life and cares of Scottish people into our cycle of worship through the year."

articles.title: Navy to commission third Mahe-class vessel INS Mangrol in Mumbai on October 12
articles.summary: Indian Navy to commission INS Mangrol, third Mahe-class ASW shallow water craft, in Mumbai on Oct 12; 80% indigenous, sonar-equipped for coastal patrols.
articles.body: Mumbai: The navy will commission INS Mangrol, the third Mahe-class anti-submarine warfare shallow water craft built by Cochin Shipyard Ltd, at the Naval Dockyard here on October 12. Built with more than 80% indigenous materials, the vessel will conduct underwater surveillance, anti-submarine exercises, mine operations, low-intensity maritime operations and coastal security missions. It will patrol coastal waters and monitor small and diesel submarines.INS Mangrol is named after a minesweeper that served the navy from 1983 to 2004. Mangrol is a historic coastal town, minor port and marine fishing harbour in Gujarat’s Junagadh district.The vessel is equipped with electronic support measures, electronics intelligence, a combat management system, DRDO’s Abhay compact hull-mounted sonar and a low frequency variable depth sonar.Its weapons include a forward-mounted rocket launcher, two triple lightweight torpedo launchers with advanced lightweight torpedoes, a 30mm naval surface gun, and two 12.7 mm stabilised remote-controlled guns. Integrated rails allow it to lay mines, while its anti-submarine warfare defence suite includes Mahindra’s torpedo decoy launching systems.The craft also has an Integrated platform management system and battle damage control system. Three marine diesel engines connected to three advanced waterjet propulsors provide a combined output of 6 MW. The system reduces underwater noise, making the vessel less susceptible to detection by enemy submarines.Built to Det Norske Veritas classification standards, INS Mangrol has a displacement of 896 to 1,100 tonnes, a beam of 11.26 and a draft of 2.7m. It can reach 25 knots, or about 46 km an hour, and has a range of 1,800 nautical miles at a cruising speed of 14 knots.The vessel has an endurance of 14 days and can accommodate 57 people, including seven officers and 50 sailors.The Ministry of defence and Cochin Shipyard Ltd signed a contract for eight ASW-SWC vessels on April 30, 2019. The first three are named after strategic coastal ports and towns: INS Mahe, INS Malvan and INS Mangrol. articles.title: Creosote found in Northumberland beach pollution investigation
articles.summary: Restrictions remain in place on Blyth Beach after a pollution incident was reported in August.
articles.body:
People are being urged not to bathe at a beach after creosote was identified in a pollution investigation.

In August, members of the public were urged not to swim at Blyth South Beach in Northumberland after reports of "oil like pollution" and a fuel smell.

Laboratory tests confirmed the substance as creosote, with investigations suggesting the cause as an ex-timber treatment works operating on land adjacent to the affected area until about 1980, Northumberland County Council said.

The council, Environment Agency (EA) and Port of Blyth said they were working to respond to the ongoing pollution, and restrictions remain in place on the land between Blyth West Pier and the Dave Stephens Centre.

An EA investigation has found the pollution is contained within an area of the beach near the Hole in the Wall, where it is seeping into the sand through contaminated groundwater.

The council said the public health risk was low, but urged people to keep their dogs away from the affected area of beach and water and to avoid contact themselves.

It is not yet known how long the clean-up will take, but it has been described as a "significant" piece of work.
